title: Qiskit — IBM's Open-Source Quantum SDK
description: Qiskit is the most widely used quantum SDK: a Python framework for building circuits, transpiling them to hardware, and running on IBM's 100+ qubit superconducting processors or high-performance simulators. Its stack spans Terra (circuits), Aer (simulators), and Runtime (hybrid execution), with Qiskit Patterns codifying reusable workflows. Open-source under Apache 2.0, it is the default entry point for learning quantum programming.

title: Cirq — Google's Quantum SDK
description: Cirq is Google's Python SDK for noisy intermediate-scale quantum computing, built around the realities of real hardware: qubits on a grid, limited connectivity, and native gate sets. It powered the 2019 quantum-supremacy experiment on Sycamore and pairs with qsim for high-performance simulation. Its moment-based circuit model maps naturally onto superconducting qubit layouts.

title: PennyLane — Quantum Machine Learning SDK
description: PennyLane by Xanadu is the SDK for quantum machine learning: it treats quantum circuits as differentiable programs and plugs them into PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX for gradient-based training. Its device abstraction runs the same code on simulators and on Xanadu's photonic hardware, Rigetti, or IBM backends. If QML finds its killer app, it will likely be prototyped in PennyLane first.

title: Strawberry Fields — Photonic Quantum SDK
description: Strawberry Fields is Xanadu's SDK for photonic continuous-variable quantum computing, where information lives in qumodes — the amplitude and phase of light — instead of two-level qubits. Gaussian gates, squeezing, and photon counting replace the usual gate set, and programs run on Xanadu's photonic chips or the built-in simulators. It is the main on-ramp to the photonic path to quantum computing.

title: t|ket> — Quantinuum's Quantum Compiler
description: t|ket> is Quantinuum's retargetable quantum compiler: it optimizes circuits — gate cancellation, commutation-based reduction, routing onto device topology — and retargets them across backends. Benchmarks consistently show it producing among the lowest two-qubit gate counts in the industry, which directly translates to less noise on real hardware. It is available as a Python package and as a compilation service.

Tens of thousands of developers have run optimization through it.

title: PyQuil — Rigetti's SDK

Quil's explicit memory model made hybrid algorithms portable before the term was fashionable.

title: Mitiq — Quantum Error Mitigation Toolkit
description: Mitiq is the open-source toolkit for error mitigation — the software techniques (zero-noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation, Clifford data regression) that squeeze useful results from noisy qubits without full error correction. It plugs into Cirq, Qiskit, PennyLane, and Braket, applying mitigation as circuit transformations. On current hardware, mitigation is often the difference between noise and signal.

title: qsim — Google's High-Performance Simulator
description: qsim is Google's C++ state-vector simulator with a Cirq front end, built for the supremacy era: it simulates 30+ qubit circuits using gate fusion, SIMD, and multi-threading. When a paper claims a quantum advantage, qsim-class tools set the bar it must beat.
